title: Oops Reversal
teaches: The Oops as we trade it: one daily candle in a leader after an orderly pullback, that opens under the prior close, trades under the prior day's low and closes back over the prior close, with a Super Oops closing over the prior high; the buy is a market order as price trades back over the prior close after the undercut, the stop sits a few cents under the Oops day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, a close back under the prior close is a warning and the stop is the exit.

walkthroughs.title: ACN, October 2006: the textbook Oops
steps: ACN, October 2006. Three weeks of drift off a fresh high, 5.0% down, to its short-term averages. Yesterday's close is the line.
October 23 it opens under that close and slips 0.73% under the prior low. Looks weak. That's the trap.
Set an alert at the prior close. It trades back over, and you buy at market, 31.51. Stop 31.12, under the low.
Close back under the prior close and it's wrong. Instead it closed over the prior high. 3R took 3 days.

walkthroughs.title: ADBE, May 2018: the undercut that tags two averages
steps: ADBE in May 2018, a leader drifting three weeks, 5.2% off its high, onto the 50-day.
May 3 it opens under the prior close and undercuts the prior low by 0.82%, right into the 50-day.
Then it trades back over the prior close. Buy at market, 221.11. Stop a few cents under the low, 218.69.
It closes over the prior high, the Super version. 3R came the very next day.

walkthroughs.title: DELL, March 2026: a deeper undercut and the widest stop
steps: Fresh off a 200-day reclaim, DELL, March 2026, drifts two weeks, 5.4% off its high. Its 50-day's still under the 200.
March 19 it digs deeper, 1.58% under the prior low. Then it rips back and closes at the high.
Buy at market as it reclaims the prior close, 149.22. Stop 146.52 under the low. 1.81% is wider, still well inside 3%.
It closed over the prior high and hit 3R the next day. That was the start of a very large run.

questions.q: It opens under yesterday's close, trades under yesterday's low, then closes back over yesterday's close. That's an Oops.
questions.why: Yes, that's the Oops. Three things, all on one daily candle. It opens under the prior close, so it starts red. It trades under yesterday's low and shakes out everyone with a stop there. Then it closes back over the prior close. That last part is the tell: buyers took it right back. Close over yesterday's high too and you've got a Super Oops, but you don't need that.

questions.why: A close over the prior high. That close swallows all of yesterday's range, so everyone who sold at any price yesterday sold lower than this. That's real strength. wrong.A few cents under the prior close: That's your buy point. A stop there gets hit on any wiggle.
wrong.A few cents under the 200-day: The 200-day tells you the trend. It's way too far away to be the stop on this trade.

questions.simple: Just under the Oops-day low. That's where the trap was set, and a trade back under it means you're wrong.
questions.story: You bought this Oops day at 221.11, right as it traded back over yesterday's close.

questions.q: In a Red market the Oops, like every long setup, is mostly cash.
questions.why: True. Green or Yellow, and Orange only for an A+ Oops. In a Red market it is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market first. Red means cash.

questions.q: In our scans, when does the Oops buy fill?
choices: On the reclaim, after the undercut
Right as it opens under the prior close
At the open, before any undercut
At the open of the next session
questions.answer: On the reclaim, after the undercut
questions.why: Our scans buy as price trades back over the prior close, once the day has traded under the prior low. It is a market order when that trigger prints, not a resting buy-stop placed at the open. No reclaim after the undercut means no trade.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut first, then the reclaim of the close. That is our scans' buy.

wrong.Right as it opens under the prior close: An open under the prior close is only the first test. The undercut and the reclaim must follow.
wrong.At the open, before any undercut: A buy at the open can fill before the undercut. Our scans wait for the reclaim.
wrong.At the open of the next session: Our scans buy on the Oops day itself, not at the next open.

questions.simple: Our scans buy as price trades back over the prior close, once the day has already traded under the prior low.

deeper.trap: Trap: calling the open under the prior close a buy. It is only the first of three tests. Our scans wait for the undercut of the prior low and then the reclaim of the prior close.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the entry trigger)

questions.q: On an Oops, you can park a buy-stop at the prior close when the bell rings and just let it fill.
questions.why: False. A buy-stop parked at the open can fill before the undercut ever happens. Say it pops up to the prior close first and only then breaks yesterday's low. Your order already filled on the wrong move. We want the undercut first, then the trade back over the close. So set an alert at the prior close and hit it with a market order when the trigger prints.
questions.lesson_line: Alert at the prior close. Market order after the undercut. No resting stop.
questions.simple: False. A resting buy-stop can fill before the undercut, so we set an alert and buy at market after it.

deeper.trap: Trap: a resting buy-stop feels careful because you do not have to watch. But it is live from the open. If price reaches its level before the day has traded under the prior low, it fills with no undercut behind it. Set an alert at the prior close and buy at market when the trigger prints.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The prior close sits ___% to 12% below the 20-day high.
questions.why: 3%. The prior close should sit 3% to 12% under the 20-day high, which is the highest high of the 20 sessions before. Under 3% is not a real pullback, with little to reverse from. Past 12% is outside the range too.
questions.lesson_line: A real pullback first: 3% to 12% off the 20-day high.
questions.simple: The pullback must be at least 3% off the 20-day high, and not past 12%.

questions.q: An Oops can fire on a dip of under 1% from the 20-day high.
questions.why: False. A real pullback comes first, 3% to 12% off the 20-day high. A dip at the highs has nothing to reverse from.
questions.lesson_line: No pullback, nothing to reverse.

questions.q: Where do you want tomorrow's low to tag?
choices: A rising 20 EMA or 50 SMA
The 5-day average, a fast read
The 9 EMA, the fast trail
The 100-day average, mid line
questions.why: A rising 20 EMA or 50-day. That's the line a leader pulls back to, and it's where I want to see buyers show up. A flag low, a gap or a round number works too. The point is a level everyone can see. The undercut shakes out the stops sitting just under it, then the reclaim leaves those sellers trapped. Here the undercut tagged a rising 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: I want the undercut to tag a level everyone can see.

wrong.The 5-day average, a fast read: Nobody trades off a 5-day line. It's noise, not a level.
wrong.The 100-day average, mid line: We don't use the 100-day. Our charts carry the 9 and 20 EMA, the 50 and the 200.
wrong.The 9 EMA, the fast trail: That's the line we trail fast movers with. For an Oops we want the deeper pullback, to the 20 or the 50.

questions.simple: A rising 20 EMA or 50 SMA, or another clear level, so the undercut has real support under it.
questions.story: This chart ends the day before an Oops. Tomorrow it dips under today's low, then closes back over today's close.

questions.q: You need a red day right before it for the Oops to count.
questions.why: False. I like a red day before it, it's a plus. But it's not one of the tests. The Oops is the open under the prior close, the trade under the prior low and the close back over. A green day before can still set one up fine.
questions.lesson_line: A red day before is a plus, not a must.
questions.simple: False. A red day before is nice to have, but the open, the undercut and the close decide it.

questions.q: An Oops prints on a huge news day, the range several times a normal candle. Is that the Oops you want?
choices: No, I want a normal-sized candle
Yes, the bigger the range the better
Only if the volume is huge too
Yes, but buy it the next morning
questions.answer: No, I want a normal-sized candle
questions.why: No. I want a technical Oops, a normal day where weak hands get shaken out and the stock gets taken right back. A huge news bar is a different animal. The news is driving it, not the pullback. And with a range that big, your stop under the low sits miles from your buy. Buying a dramatic, news-sized Oops day is a mistake.
questions.lesson_line: A clean technical candle, not a news bar.

wrong.Yes, the bigger the range the better: A huge range puts the Oops-day low far under your buy. That's a wide stop and fewer shares.
wrong.Only if the volume is huge too: Volume can raise the grade, but it's never a must. The size of the news bar is the problem.
wrong.Yes, but buy it the next morning: Buying the day after a news bar is a delayed-reaction trade, a different setup than the Oops.

questions.simple: No. A huge news bar puts your stop far away, and the move is about news, not a clean shakeout.

reasons: a threshold from the card that is still proposed

questions.q: An Oops needs a big surge in volume on the reversal day to count.
questions.why: False. Volume isn't one of the tests. The open under the close, the undercut of yesterday's low and the close back over decide it. If volume picks up on the reclaim, I like it. It raises the grade. A quiet reclaim still counts.
questions.lesson_line: Volume raises the grade. The undercut and the reclaim are the test.
questions.simple: False. Volume can raise the grade, but the open, the undercut and the close decide the Oops.

questions.q: How much comes off at the first trim, 3R?
choices: A third
Half
All of it
A quarter
questions.why: A third. The hard rule is a third at 3R, another third at 5R, then trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, and trail the last third.

wrong.Half: The hard rule is a third, not half.
wrong.All of it: Trims are thirds. The last third is trailed.
wrong.A quarter: The hard rule is a third at 3R.

questions.q: Where's your 3R mark?
questions.why: 157.32. Your R is what you risk on one share: 149.22 minus 146.52 is 2.70. Stack three of those on top of your 149.22 fill and you're at 157.32. Mark it before the open so you know where you stand. But it's a mark on the ruler, not a sell order. This one ran through it the very next day, and we very rarely sell that early.
questions.lesson_line: Know where 3R is before the open. It's a mark, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 157.32, your fill plus three times the 2.70 you're risking on each share.

deeper.example: DELL on 2026-03-19. The stop was 1.81% under the buy, and 3R printed the very next session. You'd still hold, since we very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy.

wrong.$154.62: You added three R to the stop, not the fill.
wrong.$151.92: That's only one R. You forgot to times it by three.
wrong.$141.12: That's three R under your fill. You went the wrong way.

questions.story: You bought this Oops day at 149.22. Your stop sits at 146.52, a few cents under the low.

questions.q: A phone alert at the Oops-day low works fine in place of a stop order, if you act on it.
questions.why: False. An alert is a message, not an order. It doesn't sell anything. You have to see it, decide and click, and that's exactly where people freeze or talk themselves into holding. A real stop order with your broker just goes. Put it in a few cents under the Oops-day low the moment you're filled.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: False, an alert only tells you price got there. A stop order with your broker actually sells.

questions.q: A clean Oops shows up on your scan. What liquidity floor does the stock have to clear before you'll even look?
choices: $10 and $20 million a day
$5 and $5 million a day
$20 and $10 million a day
$10 and 1 million shares a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million traded a day. Under that, I don't care how good the candle looks. Thin names gap, trade with wide spreads and won't let you out at your stop. Price times average daily volume gives you the dollars traded, so you can check it in a few seconds.
questions.lesson_line: Ten bucks a share, twenty million a day. Under that, I'm not watching.

wrong.$5 and $5 million a day: Way too thin. Names like that spread wide and jump your stop.
wrong.$20 and $10 million a day: Flipped. It's $10 a share and $20 million a day.
wrong.$10 and 1 million shares a day: We count dollars traded, not shares. A million shares of a $10 stock is only $10 million.

questions.simple: At least $10 a share and $20 million a day. Thin stocks won't let you out cleanly.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23) and a held decision (D-030)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never buy an Oops more than ___% above the prior close.
questions.why: 4%. We never buy more than 4% above the prior close, the buy point. Past that you are chasing. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the prior close and I am done.
questions.simple: Never pay more than 4% over the prior close, because past that you are chasing.

questions.q: Why does the stop sit under the Oops-day low?
choices: It marks where the trap was set
It keeps the loss at exactly 3%
It is the prior day's low
It is the low of the last 20 days
questions.answer: It marks where the trap was set
questions.why: It marks where the trap was set. A trade below the Oops-day low is the stop, and the stop is the exit. It is not a fixed percent. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, but the Oops-day low sets it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the Oops-day low the trap has failed. That is the exit.

wrong.It keeps the loss at exactly 3%: About 3% is only where the stop usually sits. The Oops-day low sets it.
wrong.It is the prior day's low: The Oops day already traded under the prior day's low. The stop goes under the Oops-day low.
wrong.It is the low of the last 20 days: That is not a rule. The stop goes under the Oops-day low, where the trap was set.

questions.simple: The stop sits there because that low is where the trap was set, so a trade below it means the trap failed.

deeper.trap: Trap: treating the 3% as the stop. Our rule says the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. That describes where it tends to land, not how to place it. Place it a few cents under the Oops-day low.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, A13)

questions.q: A Super Oops only needs the day's high to pass the prior high.
questions.why: False. A Super Oops is any Oops that closes over the prior high, so the whole prior day is engulfed. A trade over the prior high during the day is not enough. The Super close is a grade mark, not a guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: The Super is a close over the prior high.
questions.simple: False, because a Super Oops needs the day to close over the prior high, not just trade over it.

questions.q: A leader's 20-day high is 100.00. Yesterday it closed at 91.50. How deep is the pullback?
questions.why: 8.5%. Take the high minus the close and divide by the high: (100.00 - 91.50) / 100.00 is 8.5%. Always measure from the high, not the close. That's a real pullback, which is what you want under an Oops. Our scans look for roughly 3% to 12% off the 20-day high. A tiny dip at the highs gives the Oops nothing to reverse.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pullback from the high. I want a real one, not a dip.
questions.simple: 8.5%, the drop from 100.00 to 91.50 divided by the high. That's a real pullback to work with.

wrong.9.3%: You divided by the close. Measure from the high.
wrong.91.5%: That's where the close sits as a share of the high. You never subtracted.

questions.q: How far is your stop from your fill?
questions.why: 1.24%. Fill minus stop is 0.39. Divide that by the 31.51 fill and you get 1.24%. That's right where I like it, in the 1-3% zone, and I'll go up to 5% when the chart calls for it. A tight stop like this buys you more shares for the same dollar risk. This was ACN in 2006, and it never looked back.
questions.lesson_line: Stop as a percent of your fill. I like 1-3%, and I'll take up to 5%.
questions.simple: 1.24%, the 0.39 gap divided by your 31.51 fill. That's a nice tight stop.

deeper.counter: DELL on 2026-03-19 had a deeper undercut, so its stop sat wider. The buy was 149.22 and the stop 146.52, which is 1.81% away. Still well inside what we like, but a wider stop means fewer shares for the same risk.

reasons: the stop range is the owner's ruling D-005

wrong.0.39%: That's the dollar gap, 0.39. You never divided by the fill.
wrong.12.4%: Decimal slip, one place too far.
wrong.98.8%: That's the stop as a share of the fill. Subtract first.

questions.story: You bought this Oops day at 31.51. Your stop is a few cents under the low, at 31.12.

questions.q: Is today an Oops day?
choices: Yes, it passes all three tests
No, it opened over the prior low
Yes, but only as a Super Oops
No, the undercut is too shallow
questions.story: Yesterday: high 50.60, low 49.40, close 50.00. Today: open 49.70, low 49.10, close 50.30.
questions.answer: Yes, it passes all three tests
questions.why: Yes. Run it test by test and you'll see it. The 49.70 open is under the 50.00 close. The 49.10 low is under the 49.40 low. The 50.30 close is back over 50.00. That's an Oops. It closed under the 50.60 high, so it's a plain one, not a Super. A plain Oops still counts.
questions.lesson_line: Check the three tests one at a time against yesterday's candle.

wrong.No, it opened over the prior low: That's only Williams' stricter version. Ours needs the open under the prior close.
wrong.Yes, but only as a Super Oops: A Super closes over the 50.60 high. This closed at 50.30, under it.
wrong.No, the undercut is too shallow: Any trade under the prior low is the undercut. How deep is a judgment call, not a test.

questions.simple: Yes. It opened under the prior close, broke the prior low and closed back over the close.

reasons: every number is in the story

questions.q: What do you call this candle?
choices: It's a Super Oops
It's a Williams Oops
A plain Oops, not a Super
It's a Kicker gap
questions.story: Yesterday: high 50.60, low 49.40, close 50.00. Today opens at 49.70, trades down to 49.10 and closes at 50.80.
questions.why: Super Oops. The 49.70 open is under the 50.00 close. The 49.10 low takes out the 49.40 low. Then it closes at 50.80, over yesterday's 50.60 high too, so the whole prior day gets swallowed. It's not Williams' version though. He wants the open under the 49.40 low, and this one opened at 49.70.
questions.lesson_line: Close over yesterday's high and you've got a Super.

wrong.It's a Williams Oops: Williams opens under the prior low. This opened at 49.70, over the 49.40 low.
wrong.A plain Oops, not a Super: It closed at 50.80, over the 50.60 high. That's the Super mark.
wrong.It's a Kicker gap: A Kicker gaps up over a red day's close. This opened down, under the close.

questions.simple: A Super Oops, because it closed over yesterday's high, not just over yesterday's close.

deeper.trap: Check the open against the right line. Williams needs an open under the prior low of 49.40. This day opened at 49.70, over it, so it is our main Oops with a Super close, not Williams' own version.

reasons: the Williams open is a held decision (D-104), only the originator's definition is used

questions.q: Which move is your buy?
choices: The 11:00 move back over 50.00
The 9:40 pop back up to 50.00
Both, each one reached 50.00
Neither, buy the next day's open
questions.story: Prior close 50.00, prior low 49.40. It opens under 50.00, pops back to 50.00 at 9:40, then breaks 49.40. At 11:00 it trades back over 50.00.
questions.why: The 11:00 move. By then it's broken the 49.40 low, so the trap's been set and sprung. Getting back over 50.00 after that is your trigger. The 9:40 pop came before any undercut. Buy that and you're just buying a bounce in a red stock. Set an alert at 50.00 and buy at market once the low has broken.
questions.lesson_line: Undercut first, then the trade back over the close. That's the buy.

wrong.The 9:40 pop back up to 50.00: Nothing had undercut yet. That's a bounce, not the trigger.
wrong.Both, each one reached 50.00: Only the move after the undercut counts. The first touch has no trap behind it.
wrong.Neither, buy the next day's open: We buy on the Oops day itself, through the trigger, not at the next open.

questions.simple: The 11:00 move, because it came after the stock broke the prior low. The early pop doesn't count.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the entry trigger)

questions.q: Do you buy it here?
choices: No, it's past 4%, that's a chase
Yes, a strong Oops keeps going
Yes, with a tighter stop to fit
No, wait for a Super close first
questions.story: Prior close 50.00. You were away from the screen and missed the reclaim. It's 11:30 and the stock is at 52.30.
questions.answer: No, it's past 4%, that's a chase
questions.why: No. At 52.30 you're more than 4% over the 50.00 buy point. That's a chase, and here's why it matters. Your stop still goes under the Oops-day low. Buy this high and the distance to it grows, so your shares shrink. A normal pullback toward 50.00 can also shake you right out. You missed it. Let it go, there's another one coming.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the buy point, you missed it. Let it go.

wrong.Yes, a strong Oops keeps going: Maybe it does. You still don't buy more than 4% over the buy point.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop to fit: The stop goes where the chart says, under the Oops-day low. Never move it up to make a trade fit.
wrong.No, wait for a Super close first: A Super close is a plus, not a must. The problem here is the chase.

questions.simple: No. You're past 4% over the buy point, so the stop is far away and the trade is a chase.

reasons: rests on the owner's no-chase rule (C28)

questions.q: Can you take it?
choices: No, a report is inside 3 days
Yes, it's an Oops, not earnings
No, never trade an earnings day
Yes, then sell before the report
questions.story: A clean Oops is reclaiming yesterday's close right now. The company reports earnings in two days.
questions.answer: No, a report is inside 3 days
questions.why: Not this one. We make no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one reports in two. A stop can't protect you from an earnings gap. The stock can open right through your stop and you eat the whole thing. Selling before the report doesn't fix it either. Let the report pass, then look again.
questions.lesson_line: Report inside 3 days, no new buy. A stop can't stop a gap.

wrong.Yes, then sell before the report: The rule is no new buy inside the window, not a quick flip around it.
wrong.Yes, it's an Oops, not earnings: The setup is fine. The calendar isn't. The report window is its own rule.
wrong.No, never trade an earnings day: An Oops on the report day itself is allowed, just graded lower. The problem is the report ahead.

questions.simple: No. A report is two days away, and a stop can't protect you from an earnings gap.

reasons: rests on the owner's earnings rule (B22)

questions.q: Three days ago it fell 6% in one session on a big red bar. Now it prints an Oops. What does that bar do to it?
choices: It takes it off my list
Nothing, that's old news
Fine, if it was a gap down
It raises the grade a bit
questions.answer: It takes it off my list
questions.why: Off the list. The pullback I want under an Oops is a quiet drift. A 6% drop three days ago is real selling, and it's still fresh. Sellers may not be done, and your Oops is trying to reverse a hit, not a rest. I'd rather wait for a clean one than buy into damage.
questions.lesson_line: I want a quiet drift into the Oops. A big red bar right before is out.

wrong.It raises the grade a bit: It does the opposite. A big red bar right before is a reason to pass.
wrong.Nothing, that's old news: Three days is fresh. That selling is still in the stock.
wrong.Fine, if it was a gap down: Gap or no gap, a drop that big is damage, not a drift.

questions.simple: Off the list. A big red bar days before means real selling, not the quiet pullback we want.

reasons: thresholds from the card that are still proposed

questions.q: What's your move at the close?
choices: Hold to the stop, don't add
Sell at the close, it failed
Add a second lot on the dip
Move the stop under 31.30
questions.story: You bought the reclaim of the 31.50 close at 31.52, stop at 31.12. The day closes at 31.30, back under 31.50 but over your stop.
questions.answer: Hold to the stop, don't add
questions.why: Hold to the stop and don't add. Closing back under 31.50 is a warning. The Oops didn't hold, and I don't love it. But 31.12 hasn't traded, and the stop is the exit. Don't bail early on a feeling, and don't throw more money at it. If it opens under 31.50 tomorrow, that's another warning. The stop still decides.
questions.lesson_line: A close back under the prior close is a warning. The stop is still the exit.

wrong.Add a second lot on the dip: Never add to a trade that's flashing a warning. One price, one stop.
wrong.Move the stop under 31.30: That's moving the stop on a feeling. The plan is 31.12, under the Oops-day low.
wrong.Sell at the close, it failed: It's a warning, not the exit. The stop at 31.12 is the exit.

questions.simple: Hold and don't add. The weak close is a warning, but your stop is still the exit.

deeper.trap: Trap: a weak close feels like a reason to act. A close under the prior close tells you the trade is wrong as an Oops. But the Oops-day stop still decides the exit. Do not sell early and do not add. Treat the next day's open below the prior close as the warning.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-003, the entry trigger)

questions.q: You're stopped out. What's your takeaway?
choices: Fine, the stop did its job
Use a wider stop next time
Skip the stop on clean ones
Decide the setup is broken
questions.story: You bought this Oops day at 67.48, stop at 66.70. Next morning it opens at 68.48, then sells straight through your stop to 66.63.
questions.answer: Fine, the stop did its job
questions.why: That's the trade working the way it should. It looked perfect, a strong close and then a gap up to 68.48 the next morning. Then it sold right through. Nothing on the chart warned you. Your stop took a planned loss of 1.16% and that's it. This was ADBE, and by early April it was down at 59.63. Without the stop, you'd be sitting in a real hole.
questions.lesson_line: A perfect-looking Oops gives no warning when it fails. The stop is the plan.

wrong.Decide the setup is broken: One stop-out isn't a verdict. Good setups lose sometimes, and the stop keeps it small.
wrong.Use a wider stop next time: A wider stop just loses more. This one kept falling to 59.63.
wrong.Skip the stop on clean ones: Clean ones fail too. This one did, with no warning at all.

questions.simple: The stop did its job. A perfect-looking Oops can still fail with no warning, and the stop keeps it small.

deeper.trap: Do not judge the trade by the result. The stop sat 1.16% under the 67.48 buy, a small planned loss. ADBE then fell to 59.63 by 04-07, so a wider stop would only have lost more.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars

questions.q: Where's your stop now?
choices: 30.85, the first 30-minute low
31.12, the original stop
Out now, the loss is past 2R
30.95, the gap-day open
questions.story: You bought at 31.52 with the stop at 31.12, so 0.40 of risk a share. Next morning it gaps open at 30.95. The first 30-minute low is 30.85, 0.67 under your buy.
questions.why: 30.85. A gap through the stop is the one time the stop moves. We let the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide, and that bar's low becomes the new stop. There's a ceiling though. If that low puts you down more than 2R, you're out. Here 0.67 down on 0.40 of risk is under 2R, so you stay in with 30.85 as the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through your stop, and the first 30 minutes set the new one.

wrong.31.12, the original stop: It already gapped through it. You can't sell at a price that isn't there.
wrong.30.95, the gap-day open: The open just tells you it gapped. The first 30 minutes decide.
wrong.Out now, the loss is past 2R: 0.67 down on 0.40 of risk is under 2R. You're still inside the ceiling.

questions.simple: 30.85. After a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30 minutes becomes the new stop.

deeper.trap: The gap price isn't the decision. The open at 30.95 only tells you it gapped. The first 30-minute bar sets the stop. Had its low put you more than 2R down, you'd get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's gap rule (B20)
the 2R check is arithmetic done by the cold checker, not a calc

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Hold it all, too early to sell
Sell a third, stop to breakeven
Sell it all and lock in 3R
Sell half, leave the stop alone
questions.story: This chart runs through the session after your buy. You bought at 149.22, stop 146.52. It's already through your 3R mark.
questions.answer: Hold it all, too early to sell
questions.why: Hold it all. This is day 1 after the buy, and we very rarely sell that early. Now look at that candle. It ran way up, then closed right on its low, on heavy volume. I don't love that. But it's still just over your 3R mark, and the stop is the exit, not one ugly candle. I'm looking for a 3, 5 or 7 day push to sell into. If you want the safety, the stop can come up to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: 3R on day 1 isn't a sell signal. Wait for the push.

wrong.Sell a third, stop to breakeven: A third at 3R isn't how we sell. The first sell is a judgment, most often day 3 or later.
wrong.Sell it all and lock in 3R: That's how you sell a big winner on day 1. We wait for the push.
wrong.Sell half, leave the stop alone: Too early. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy.

questions.simple: Hold it all. We almost never sell on day 1, and the first sell is a judgment into a push.

reasons: held decision D-019 on the breakeven

questions.q: When do you take the first trim?
choices: Right away, at the open
At the close, if it holds
On a dip back to 52.40
After the first 30-minute bar closes
questions.story: You hold an Oops with a 3R level of 52.40. The next morning the stock opens at 53.10.
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. Your 3R level is 52.40 and the stock opened at 53.10, past it, so the first third comes off right there. Do not wait for the close or for a dip.
questions.lesson_line: Open past the level, take the trim at the open.

wrong.At the close, if it holds: The rule is to take it at the open, not to wait for the close.
wrong.On a dip back to 52.40: The stock already opened past 52.40. Take the trim at the open, because the dip may never come.
wrong.After the first 30-minute bar closes: The first 30 minutes decide a gap against the stop. A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

questions.simple: Take the first third at the open, because the stock opened at 53.10, past the 3R level of 52.40.

questions.q: Keep it or cut it?
choices: Sell it, find a better setup
Hold for the 5R push
Add on a break of the range
Widen the stop for more room
questions.story: Ten trading days in. The Oops has chopped sideways and sits at +0.5R. The stop has never been touched.
questions.answer: Sell it, find a better setup
questions.why: Sell it. Ten days and it still hasn't made 1R. That's our time stop. The good ones get going within a few days. One that just chops is tying up money you could have in something that's moving. Take the small gain and go find the next one.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R, I'm out. Money goes where it's working.

wrong.Widen the stop for more room: A stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Hold for the 5R push: There's no push. Ten days under 1R is the time stop.
wrong.Add on a break of the range: Ten days and it hasn't worked. That doesn't earn more money. We buy once, at one price.

questions.simple: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after ten days gets cut, so your money goes to something working.

deeper.example: Ten days at +0.5R means the trade is barely paying you for the risk. Holding for 5R keeps the money stuck in it. Selling frees it for the next setup.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-019, the time stop)

questions.q: Williams' exit, the first profitable open, is our exit.
questions.why: False. Williams' bailout exits on the first profitable open, even for 1c of profit. We very rarely sell on day 1; our first sell is a judgment, and the rest trails.
questions.lesson_line: Williams' exit is his. Ours is a judged first sell and a trail.
questions.simple: No. Williams sells at the first profitable open, but our first sell is a judgment, rarely on day 1.

reasons: the Williams half rests on a Radge page that blocked this run's fetch
rests on the owner's exit plan (E51)

questions.q: Which Oops trades can you take today?
choices: Just an A+ Oops, at most
Any A or A+, at full risk
Any Oops, but at half size
None, Orange means all cash
questions.story: A clean Oops is reclaiming the close. Our market reading, the app's Green to Red filter, says Orange: the market's under pressure, one step from Red.
questions.answer: Just an A+ Oops, at most
questions.why: Just an A+. In Orange, setups fail more often because the market isn't backing them. So I only want my very best, the cleanest Oops with the tightest risk. That's what A+ means to us, the kind we size up on. The A and the B can wait for a better market. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange, A+ only. Yellow, smaller. Green, press. Red, mostly cash.

wrong.Any A or A+, at full risk: An A waits in Orange, and full risk is for Green.
wrong.Any Oops, but at half size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Orange is only A+.
wrong.None, Orange means all cash: Mostly cash is Red. Orange still allows your best setup.

questions.simple: Only an A+. In Orange, setups fail more, so you take just your very best one.

questions.q: Your Oops worked and you've sold some into the push. It's a steady mover, not a rocket. What do you trail the rest with?
choices: The 20 EMA
The 50-day
The 200-day
The 9 EMA
questions.why: The 20 EMA. Fast movers get the 9 EMA, steadier names get the 20. Sell what's left on a close below it. The 9 is too tight for a steady stock, it'll shake you out on a normal dip. The 50 hands back way too much of the move.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steady name, 20 EMA. Sell on a close below.

wrong.The 50-day: Too loose. You'd hand back a big piece of the move.
wrong.The 200-day: That's the trend line, not a trail. Way too far away.
wrong.The 9 EMA: That's for fast movers. A steady name dips under it and shakes you out.

questions.simple: The 20 EMA. Steady names trail it, and you sell the rest on a close below it.

questions.q: In our data, the Oops-day low broke within 20 sessions on about three of every four Oops days.
questions.why: True, about 75% of them. The best ones never look back, but most Oops lows do get taken out within a month or so. So you don't buy an Oops and hope. You put the stop under the low and let it do its work. When the low holds, great. When it breaks, you're out small and on to the next one.
questions.lesson_line: Most Oops lows break sooner or later. The stop is the plan.
questions.simple: True. Most Oops lows break within a month, which is why the stop is the plan.

deeper.counter: Counter-example: ADBE on 2014-03-12 looked perfect. It opened 1.5% up the next morning and then sold straight through the Oops-day low. A perfect-looking day gives no warning, so the stop is the whole plan, even when the day looks like the best example.

reasons: a data statistic that changes with the data

questions.q: Do you take the long?
choices: Pass, stay mostly in cash
Pass, put half the account in shorts
Take it at full risk anyway
Take it smaller, like Yellow
questions.story: A clean Oops is reclaiming yesterday's close. Our market reading, the app's Green to Red filter, is Red.
questions.why: Pass. In Red I'm mostly in cash. One clean candle doesn't change what the whole market is doing, and setups fail a lot more when the market's selling off. You don't need to be the hero here. Wait for the reading to improve. That's when Oops setups start paying again.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, I'm mostly cash. The Oops can wait.

wrong.Pass, put half the account in shorts: Red is mostly cash. Shorts below the 200-day can be part of it, but half the account in shorts isn't mostly cash.
wrong.Take it at full risk anyway: Full risk is for Green. A clean candle doesn't fix a Red market.
wrong.Take it smaller, like Yellow: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Red is mostly cash.

questions.simple: Pass. A Red market means mostly cash, and one clean Oops doesn't change that.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D46, F65)

questions.q: How do you handle that new high?
choices: Buy only on a new trigger
Buy it back, you were right
Widen your stop next time
Never touch it again
questions.story: You bought this Oops day at 176.35, stop 174.16. The next day it fell through the stop. A few weeks later the stock runs to a fresh high.
questions.answer: Buy only on a new trigger
questions.why: Buy only on a new trigger. The stop did its job the next day. Seeing the high weeks later and calling the stop wrong is hindsight. That later move is a different trade. If the setup triggers again, you take it fresh, with its own entry, its own stop and every rule. V did get there, but from a later entry.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is the plan working. Back in only on a new trigger.

wrong.Buy it back, you were right: Being early isn't being right. You need a new trigger.
wrong.Widen your stop next time: A wider stop just means bigger losses on the ones that don't come back.
wrong.Never touch it again: Nothing's wrong with the stock. Take it again if it sets up again.

questions.simple: Only buy again on a new trigger, with a new stop. The old trade ended at the stop.

deeper.trap: Seeing the later peak and calling the stop a mistake is hindsight. A few weeks later is a different trade. Buying it back needs its own trigger, its own stop and every rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's re-entry rule (B21)

questions.q: The 2R and 3R targets the app draws on an Oops are where we sell.
questions.why: False. Those marks are a ruler, not the plan. Our first sell is a judgment. We very rarely sell on day 1, and we like to sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. On a strong Oops that can be 5 to 10R. Sell at 2R every time and you cap your best trades.
questions.lesson_line: The app's 2R and 3R are a ruler, not the sell plan.
questions.simple: False, the app's marks are only a ruler. We sell into a push by judgment, not at a fixed target.

deeper.trap: Trap: the app shows 2R and 3R, so they look official. Our first sell is a judgment, often into a push of 3, 5 or 7 days, then a trail.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: An Oops above a rising 200-day is a better trade than one above a falling 200-day.
questions.why: True. A rising 200-day means the long-term trend is behind you. The simple check is whether it sits higher than it did 20 sessions ago. It's a plus we like to see, not a must. The hard line is a different one. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks at all.
questions.lesson_line: A rising 200-day under it is a better floor. Under the 200, no buy.
questions.simple: True. A rising 200-day means the big trend is with you, so the Oops has a better floor.

questions.q: What are you looking at here?
choices: An Oops, on yesterday's low
A 2B, it reclaimed same day
A U&R, it undercut a key level
A Kicker, it gapped up
questions.story: Yesterday: low 83.10, close 83.90. Today opens at 83.50, trades under 83.10 and closes at 84.40. There is no older swing low nearby.
questions.why: An Oops. It opened at 83.50, under the 83.90 close. It broke yesterday's 83.10 low and closed back over the close at 84.40. All in one candle, off yesterday's low. A 2B needs an older swing low, and there isn't one nearby. A U&R needs a bigger level than yesterday's low. So you're looking at an Oops.
questions.lesson_line: Check which low broke. Yesterday's low, in one candle, means Oops.

wrong.A U&R, it undercut a key level: A U&R needs a bigger level, like a rising average or a base low. Yesterday's low is Oops territory.
wrong.A Kicker, it gapped up: A Kicker gaps up over a red close. This opened down.
wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed same day: A 2B takes out an older swing low. This only broke yesterday's.

questions.simple: An Oops. It broke only yesterday's low and got back over the close the same day.

deeper.counter: Same shape, different level. Had it broken an older swing low and closed back over it a session or two later, it would be a 2B. Breaking only yesterday's low and reclaiming the close in one candle is an Oops.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria cards

questions.q: Oops or not?
choices: No, it's a 2B on an older low
Yes, it reclaimed within 3 sessions
Yes, it broke a low and took it back
No, it's a Red to Green
questions.story: On Monday the stock breaks a swing low from twelve sessions ago. It closes back above that low on Tuesday. Tuesday never trades under Monday's low.
questions.answer: No, it's a 2B on an older low
questions.why: No, you've got a 2B. Monday broke a swing low from twelve sessions back, not yesterday's low. And it took until Tuesday to close back over it. The Oops is one candle off yesterday's low. A 2B breaks an older swing low and can take a day or a few to get back above it.
questions.lesson_line: Yesterday's low in one candle is an Oops. An older low over a day or two is a 2B.

wrong.Yes, it reclaimed within 3 sessions: That's the 2B's window. The Oops is judged on one candle.
wrong.Yes, it broke a low and took it back: Wrong low. An Oops breaks yesterday's low, not one from twelve sessions ago.
wrong.No, it's a Red to Green: A Red to Green is just a trade back through the prior close. This reclaimed an old swing low.

questions.simple: No. It broke an old swing low and took two days to get back, so it's a 2B.

deeper.trap: The reclaim looks like an Oops, so count two things: how old the broken low is, and how many candles it took. An older swing low and a day or two to get back above it is a 2B.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria cards

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A U&R
An Oops
A Kicker
A 2B
questions.story: The stock dips under its rising 50-day average and closes back above it the next day. It never traded under the prior day's low on the reclaim day.
questions.why: A U&R, an undercut and reclaim. The level here is a rising 50-day, a bigger level than yesterday's low. That's U&R territory, and its reclaim can take a few sessions. Your Oops has to trade under yesterday's low and get back over the close on the same candle. This one never traded under the prior low.
questions.lesson_line: Bigger level, a few days: U&R. Yesterday's low, one candle: Oops.

wrong.A Kicker: A Kicker gaps up. This dipped under an average.
wrong.An Oops: It never traded under the prior day's low on the reclaim day. No undercut, no Oops.
wrong.A 2B: A 2B breaks a swing low. This broke a rising average.

questions.simple: A U&R. It undercut a rising average and took it back, a bigger level than yesterday's low.

deeper.trap: Trap: the speed of the reclaim. Closing back above the level the next day looks like an Oops. But an Oops must trade under the prior day's low in one candle. The level is the tell. Yesterday's low is an Oops. An older swing low is a 2B. A bigger level, like the rising 50-day in this story, is a U&R.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-101, the 2B and U&R levels)

questions.q: Oops or something else?
choices: A Kicker, opened over the close
An Oops, it closed over the high
A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low
A Red to Green, it turned green
questions.story: Yesterday was a red day: it opened at 52.00, closed at 50.00 and its high was 52.40. Today the stock opens at 50.90 and closes at 52.80.
questions.answer: A Kicker, opened over the close
questions.why: A Kicker. Yesterday was red, closing at 50.00. Today opened at 50.90, already over that close. That's a gap up. An Oops does the opposite: it opens down under the prior close, takes out the low, then comes back. The 52.80 close over the 52.40 high looks Oops-like, but you check the open first.
questions.lesson_line: Check the open first. Gap up is a Kicker. Open down is where an Oops starts.

wrong.An Oops, it closed over the high: An Oops opens down under the prior close. This opened over it.
wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low: Nothing broke a swing low here. It opened higher.
wrong.A Red to Green, it turned green: It never started red. It opened over the prior close.

questions.simple: A Kicker. It gapped up over a red day's close, and an Oops opens down instead.

deeper.trap: The close over the prior high tempts you to say Oops. But an Oops opens down under the prior close. The direction of the gap is the first test.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria card

questions.q: What did that last day give you?
choices: A Red to Green, not an Oops
An Oops, it closed over the close
A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low
A Kicker, it reclaimed the close
questions.story: The last day on the chart. It opens under the prior close and closes over it. Its low stays 0.48% above the prior day's low.
questions.answer: A Red to Green, not an Oops
questions.why: A Red to Green, not an Oops. It opened under the close and finished over it. But the low held 0.48% above yesterday's low, so nothing got undercut. No trap, no Oops. Every Oops is a Red to Green, but not every Red to Green is an Oops. This was GOOGL on 2026-02-27: a 303.80 low against a 302.35 prior low.
questions.lesson_line: No trade under yesterday's low, no Oops. It's just a Red to Green.

wrong.An Oops, it closed over the close: Close, but no undercut. The low never got under yesterday's low.
wrong.A Kicker, it reclaimed the close: A Kicker gaps up over a red close. This opened down.

questions.simple: A Red to Green. It never traded under yesterday's low, and the Oops needs that undercut first.

deeper.trap: GOOGL on 2026-02-27 opened at 304.14, under the 307.38 prior close, and closed at 311.76. Yet its low of 303.80 held above the prior low of 302.35. The open and the close looked right. The undercut was missing.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars

questions.q: Oops or Go Signal?
choices: A Go Signal, it fires on the hourly
An Oops, undercut a slight range
A Kicker, a gap up over a close
A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low
questions.story: After a catalyst gap, a stock digests in an hourly flag. It undercuts a slight range and goes red to green in the first hour.
questions.answer: A Go Signal, it fires on the hourly
questions.why: A Go Signal. It fires on the hourly chart, off a little flag after a catalyst gap. The Oops lives on the daily candle: under yesterday's low, then back over yesterday's close. Both go red to green, which is why people mix them up. Look at which chart you're reading.
questions.lesson_line: Daily candle, Oops. Hourly flag, Go Signal.

wrong.An Oops, undercut a slight range: The Oops undercuts yesterday's daily low, not a small range on the hourly.
wrong.A Kicker, a gap up over a close: A Kicker is a daily gap up over a red day.
wrong.A 2B, it reclaimed a swing low: A 2B breaks a swing low. This undercut a small range inside an hourly flag.

questions.simple: A Go Signal. It forms on an hourly flag, and the Oops is read on the daily candle.

deeper.trap: Red to green appears in both. A Go Signal goes red to green inside an hourly flag after a catalyst gap. An Oops is one daily candle that undercuts the prior day's low and reclaims the prior close. Same words, different chart.

reasons: the tell between lookalikes comes from the criteria card

questions.q: Would you buy this one?
choices: No, it's a delayed reaction
Yes, it passes all three tests
Yes, the news drop makes it stronger
No, the undercut is too shallow
questions.story: The last candle is the reversal day. The prior day fell from 126.58 to 118.08 on news. Today it opens under that close, undercuts the low by 12 cents and closes just over the prior close.
questions.why: No. The day before fell 6.71% on news, 126.58 to 118.08. That isn't a quiet pullback, it's a news hit. A bounce the next day is a delayed reaction, a different setup. The candle passes all three tests, but what's behind it is wrong. This was PANW in 2023. I'd pass on this all day.
questions.lesson_line: A bounce the day after a news drop isn't an Oops.

wrong.Yes, it passes all three tests: The candle passes. The day before doesn't. A news drop isn't the pullback we want.
wrong.No, the undercut is too shallow: 12 cents under is still an undercut. The news day is the problem.
wrong.Yes, the news drop makes it stronger: A big drop right before takes it off the list.

questions.simple: No. The day before was a big news drop, so this bounce is a delayed reaction, not an Oops.

deeper.trap: All three tests pass, so it looks like an Oops. The problem is the day before: a 6.71% fall on news. PANW's undercut was only 12 cents and its close was just 0.5% over the prior close. The day after a news day is a delayed reaction.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars
the orderly-pullback criterion is still proposed

questions.q: Which rule fails?
choices: No pullback: it sits at the highs
The undercut is missing
The close is under the prior close
The stop is over 3%
questions.story: The stock opens under the prior close, undercuts the prior low and closes over the prior close. The prior close was 0.6% under the 20-day high.
questions.answer: No pullback: it sits at the highs
questions.why: No pullback. The prior close was only 0.6% under the 20-day high, a dip at the highs with nothing to reverse from. That was HD on 2025-09-15.
questions.lesson_line: A dip at the highs is not a pullback.

wrong.The undercut is missing: The stock did undercut the prior low.
wrong.The close is under the prior close: It closed over the prior close.
wrong.The stop is over 3%: The failing rule is the pullback, not the stop.

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, it's way under the 200-day
No, it's only a plain Oops
No, the day before wasn't red
Yes, the candle passes the tests
questions.story: A clean Oops candle is the last day on the chart. Prior close 66.97, Oops close 67.23. The 200-day SMA sits at 76.48.
questions.why: No. Both closes sit about 12% under the 200-day. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks, period. That's a hard line. A stock down there is in a downtrend, and an Oops in a downtrend is just a bounce. Indexes and levered ETFs are the only exception, never a single stock. This was BABA in 2016. Watch it, don't buy it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, an Oops is just a bounce. We don't buy it.

wrong.No, it's only a plain Oops: A plain Oops is still an Oops. A Super close is a plus, not a must.
wrong.No, the day before wasn't red: A red day before is nice, not required.
wrong.Yes, the candle passes the tests: The candle's fine. The stock is 12% under its 200-day, and that's a hard no.

questions.simple: No, it's far under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks down there. Watch it only.

deeper.trap: BABA's Oops-day close was 67.23 against a 200-day of 76.48. The candle was clean, but the candle is only one test. The 200-day comes first, and for a stock it's a hard no.

questions.q: Is this Williams' version of the Oops?
choices: No, it opened above the prior low
Yes, it opened under the close
Yes, it undercut the prior low
No, it didn't close over the high
questions.story: Yesterday: high 82.40, low 80.60, close 81.20. Today: open 80.90, low 80.10, close 81.70.
questions.answer: No, it opened above the prior low
questions.why: No. Williams wants the open under yesterday's low, and this opened at 80.90, over the 80.60 low. You've still got an Oops by our main test though. It opened under the 81.20 close, dipped to 80.10 and closed back over at 81.70. Ours only needs the open under the close.
questions.lesson_line: Williams opens under the low. Our main Oops opens under the close.

wrong.Yes, it opened under the close: That's our main version. Williams needs the open under the low.
wrong.Yes, it undercut the prior low: Every Oops does that. Williams also opens under the low.
wrong.No, it didn't close over the high: Closing over the high is the Super mark. It has nothing to do with Williams.

questions.simple: No, Williams opens under the prior low. This one opened over it, so it's our main Oops instead.

deeper.counter: To be Williams' version this day needed to open under 80.60, the prior low. It opened at 80.90. Every other test still holds, which is why it stays our main Oops.

reasons: held decision D-104 on the Williams open

questions.q: What did that Super close get you?
choices: A better grade, nothing more
A confirmed new uptrend
Room to give the stop more space
A trade that's safe from the stop
questions.story: This chart ends on the Oops day, a Super Oops closing at 167.00 over the 166.53 high. You bought at 157.19, stop 155.55. Next day it opens at 165.36 and falls to 151.52.
questions.why: A better grade, nothing more. AMAT closed at 167.00 over the 166.53 high, about as good a close as you'll see. The next day it was a 9% drop right through your 155.55 stop. A Super close tells you buyers showed up. It doesn't promise they stay. Your stop is the same whatever the close looked like.
questions.lesson_line: A Super close raises the grade. It doesn't guarantee the trade.

wrong.A confirmed new uptrend: One close confirms nothing. It fell 9% the next day.
wrong.Room to give the stop more space: A stop never moves wider, however good the close.
wrong.A trade that's safe from the stop: It went straight through the stop the next day.

questions.simple: A better grade, nothing more. Even a Super Oops can fail the next day, so the stop stays put.

deeper.trap: AMAT on 2022-01-14 had the best-looking close of the set, 167.00 over the 166.53 prior high. The next day was a 9% down day through the 155.55 stop, the first of three straight down days. A grade mark does not move the stop.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars

questions.q: What did the stock's own chart not show you?
choices: The market wasn't Green
The undercut was too small
The close was too weak
The stop was too wide
questions.story: This chart ends on the Oops day. It undercut the prior low by 1.26% and closed at 0.85 of its range. You bought at 74.97, stop 73.73. It's stopped out the next day, and the index goes on to a lower low.
questions.why: The market wasn't Green. On its own chart this was mostly fine: a 1.26% undercut, a strong close and a 1.65% stop. One flaw: the 50-day was still a hair under the 200-day, just crossing up. The bigger problem was SPY. It was rolling over, and it made a lower low a few days later. You check the market reading before every buy, not after the stop. A good chart in a bad market fails a lot more often.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart can't tell you what the market's doing. Check the reading first.

wrong.The close was too weak: It closed at 0.85 of its range. That's strong.
wrong.The stop was too wide: 1.65% from the buy is right where we like it.
wrong.The undercut was too small: 1.26% under the prior low is a real undercut.

questions.simple: The market wasn't Green. The stock's chart looked fine, but the index kept falling.

deeper.trap: UBER on 2025-03-07: buy 74.97, stop 73.73, 1.65% away. It was stopped the next day, and the stock was 63.94 four weeks later. A clean daily chart cannot show the market reading, so check the reading before the buy, not after the stop.

reasons: a dated example read off our own bars
rebuilt from the dossier row so every number is in a cited quote

questions.q: Your move after the stop-out?
choices: Take the loss; the setup was right
Move the stop lower next time
Rewrite the rules after one stop-out
Buy it right back at the open
questions.story: A clean Oops with a red prior day, a pullback to the 21-day and a strong close. Two days later it trades under the Oops-day low and you are stopped out.
questions.answer: Take the loss; the setup was right
questions.why: Take the planned loss. A good example can have a horrible result: our own named cases are WFRD and SEI. Do not expect every Oops to work. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. Buy again only on a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A good setup can lose. The loss was planned.

wrong.Move the stop lower next time: A stop never moves down or wider.
wrong.Rewrite the rules after one stop-out: One loss on a good setup is part of the system.
wrong.Buy it right back at the open: Buy again only on a new trigger.

questions.simple: A clean setup can still lose, so take the planned loss and keep your rules.

deeper.trap: Judging the rules by one result. WFRD and SEI were good examples with horrible results. A good setup lost, the stop did its job, and the rules stay as they are.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop rule (A4)

questions.q: What went wrong?
choices: Nothing; a Super close is no guarantee
The stop was too tight
You should have bought the close
The prior day was not red
questions.story: A Super Oops closes over the prior high with a 1.52% stop. The next day it opens a little lower and sells through the stop.
questions.answer: Nothing; a Super close is no guarantee
questions.why: Nothing went wrong with the rules. CRM was a Super Oops on 2023-06-20 and sold through the stop the next day. The Super close is a grade mark.
questions.lesson_line: A clean Oops can still fail. The stop is the plan.

wrong.The stop was too tight: The stop sits under the Oops-day low, not where the day felt safe.
wrong.You should have bought the close: The close is not the entry.
wrong.The prior day was not red: A red prior day is preferred, not required.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job: a small planned loss
Cost you the trade; it needed room
